placeholders.days: whole days since the relevant event — the student's last visit, a past failure on this problem, or the length of the current unbroken practice streak
placeholders.streak: number of consecutive correct drills in the current run
placeholders.attempts: how many attempts the student previously needed on this problem
placeholders.secret: the name of the secret currently being taught or tested
placeholders.idiom: the C++ expression at the heart of the current secret
placeholders.requirement: name of the gate dimension that is short: recognition, understanding, implementation, or retention
placeholders.shortfall: how far the short gate dimension sits below its threshold, as a percentage
placeholders.score: how many final-test problems were answered correctly
placeholders.total: number of problems in the final test
placeholders.required: how many must be answered correctly to pass

greeting_first: Two thousand one hundred and forty-seven million, four hundred and eighty-three thousand, six hundred and forty-seven. — Sit down. That is where your machine stops counting, and everything I teach you here is about what it does afterwards.
Another one. — They arrive able to write a modulus and unable to say which of the four operations it survives. Sit. We will find out which kind you are.
You will find the algorithms in this temple very short and the corrections very long. That ratio is not an accident and it is not my fault.
I talk to the room. Do not take it personally; the room has been here longer than either of us and it has heard the wrong answers before.
greeting_returning: Again. — Recite the boundary of a signed 64-bit integer before we start.
Sit. The remainder is where you left it.
You came back. — Most of them come back until the first overflow, which they never see, and then they stop coming back for reasons they cannot name.
greeting_after_gap: {days} days. — The primes were not lonely. Sit.
Gone {days} days. What decays first is not the loop. It is the arithmetic underneath it, which you were never watching in the first place.
{days} days away. Very well: minus three, modulo seven. Say it before you sit.
{days} days. — I have had students return after a year and remember the descent perfectly and still type `int`. We start with the types.
lesson_intro: {secret}. Four lines. Read the arithmetic under them and not the lines.
I will give you the numbers. — I always give them the numbers. They write them in the margin and then they write `int` anyway, and then they come back and tell me the judge is broken.
This one is short enough to memorise and subtle enough to get wrong for a year. Both of those are true at once and that is the difficulty.
Watch what is FORMED before you watch what is computed. That distinction is the whole temple.
lesson_memorise: Take `{idiom}` whole. Do not reconstruct it under a clock — reconstruction is where the outer reduction goes missing.
Memorise this one as a single token. — It is not an expression. It is a word.
Keep it. You will write it in nearly every problem in this region and in half the problems outside it.
This goes in the hand. What it protects you from goes somewhere you will have to keep looking at.
drill_correct: Good. — They always get that one.
drill_wrong: No. The product is formed before the remainder arrives. Read the precedence again.
Wrong. Minus three modulo seven is minus three in this language. You are thinking in a different one.
No. That is a sum of residues in an int, and two of them fit and three of them do not, which is why you believed it.
Wrong. You reduced the exponent by the modulus. The exponent lives in a group of order m minus one.
No. Fermat wants a prime. You gave it a composite and it answered you politely.
Wrong. That multiplication happened before the division, and the answer was never the problem — the product was.
No. — And that is the one I warn about in the opening speech, every intake, without exception.
drill_streak: {streak} in a row. The hand is quick. I am still watching the types.
Steady. — Speed here means nothing; there is no shape to see, only arithmetic to respect.
trial_intro: Nothing named. Read the CONSTRAINTS before the statement — that is where I hid the answer and where the setter hid theirs.
One problem. The bounds are the whole message.
The label comes off. The arithmetic does not.
Decide what cannot be formed, and then decide what to do instead. In that order.
fail_wrong_pattern: Wrong tool. Nothing there needed factorising — a common divisor was wanted and the descent gives it in ninety steps where you asked for a billion.
No. That exponent was given, not discovered. You went looking for primes in a statement that had already told you the power.
You reduced when you should have descended. The modulus was not given to you; it was the thing being asked for.
No. — They see a large number and reach for the sieve. There is no sieve to 10^12. There never was.
fail_timeout: Time. — Nothing you had was wrong. You were checking the arithmetic by hand, which is the right instinct and the slow one. Drills fix that.
Time ran out. You knew it. Knowing it slowly is fluency, and fluency is repetition. Nothing is lost.
Time. You spent it deriving the inverse formula. Memorise it and spend the time on the constraints instead.
fail_wrong_answer: The method was right and the type was not. Test seven is where two billion lives.
Correct approach. You subtracted and printed a negative number where a residue was demanded. One expression, three operations, and you wrote two of them.
You had it. The accumulator wrapped — every term fitted and the sum did not, which is the quiet version and the one nobody catches by rereading.
Right idea, wrong exponent. p minus one gives you the number one. It is a very believable number.
The reduction was missing between the two multiplications, so the expression formed a product of three residues. Ten to the twenty-seven. — Nobody has that type.
You divided before you multiplied. Or rather you multiplied before you divided, which is the same sentence read from the correct end.
success: Done. — The next one gives less away in the constraints.
success_fast: Fast, and you checked the bound before you typed. That is the right order.
You saw the modulus and reached for the wider type without being told. Good.
No hesitation and no overflow. Those two together are rarer than you think.
Quick. — And correct, which is the half that matters.
praise_exceptional: That was well done. You found the boundary before you crossed it.
You checked the types against the constraints unprompted. — Most of them never do that once.
Clean, and safe at the edges. I noticed the order in which you decided those.
That is the best work you have done here. You reasoned about what could be FORMED, not merely about what was computed.
praise_major: I have taught a great many students to write a modulus and perhaps four of them to respect it. You are one of the four. You have earned my respect.

You arrived able to reduce a number. You leave able to say exactly which multiplication in your program is the one that will kill it. That is the rarer skill by a long way. You have earned my respect.
I do not say this often and I will not repeat it: you now check the arithmetic before the algorithm. Everything after this temple is safer because of it. You have earned my respect.
memorisation_detected: You remember which expression this problem wanted. You cannot say what it protects against. — Those are different things, and the difference is the entire temple. A different problem.
You pass the ones you have seen and fail their variants. Change the modulus from 10^9 to 10^18 and you are lost, which means you learned a line and not a bound.
You wrote the repair without the second reduction, on a problem where it did not matter. It will matter. Back one step.
improvement_noticed: You failed this {days} days ago on an overflow. Today the types were right before the algorithm was. That is improvement.
You needed {attempts} attempts on this once. Today, one. — I keep a record. It is the only thing in this temple that is not arithmetic.
This is the problem where you printed a negative residue for an hour. You did not, today.
Straighter than last time. You read the constraints first, which is a habit and not a talent, which is why I can take some credit for it.
commitment_noticed: {days} days unbroken. — Arithmetic rewards the patient more reliably than the quick. It is one of the few honest things about it.
Many arrive at this temple. Most of them want the four lines and not the boundary, and most of them leave when I ask for the boundary. You have not.
You have returned after every failure so far. Noted.
Talent walks in here weekly and walks out with an int accumulator. Attendance is the part I cannot teach; you brought your own.
gate_locked: Not yet. {requirement} is short by {shortfall} percent. Return when it is not.
The gate holds. Understanding is short — you produce the expression and cannot say which of its three operations you would lose first.
No. Recognition is short. You know four techniques and cannot yet tell from a statement which one it is describing, and the constraints are telling you plainly.
Implementation is short. The reasoning is sound and the types are not, which in this region is the same as being wrong.
Retention is short. — Of everything I teach, the sign of the remainder is what goes first. It always is. Review, then the gate.
gate_open: The gate is open. Come when you are ready and not when you are impatient.
Nothing is short any more. The final test waits.
You meet the requirements. — The decision from here is yours; I am only the arithmetic.
final_test_intro: I will name nothing. Every drill before this existed so that I would not have to.
{total} problems, and {required} of them must be right. Read the constraints twice. That is not encouragement; it is the method.
No help. Only the statements, and whatever bound you can still compute in your head.
One of these has a modulus past three thousand and thirty-seven million. — I am not going to tell you which.
victory: It is done. The temple is behind you.
You passed. — Remember the boundaries, not only the four lines. The lines are in every editorial; the boundaries are in none of them.
Finished. Everything after this assumes you can look at a multiplication and say whether it fits. You can.
That is mastery of the leftover. Nothing you meet later will be shorter, and nothing will be quieter when it goes wrong. Go.
